title: Making plans with friends
goal: Ask a friend if they're free, suggest what to do and where to meet, hurry them up, say you're on your way or running late, and cancel without offending anyone.
intro:
From here on, the course is about the Pashto you'll use with friends. Part 2 starts with the most social thing there is: making plans. Is your friend free tonight? Shall we go out to eat, to the park, to a film? Where shall we meet — and why is he *still* not here?

You'll learn the 'we' subjunctive for **let's** and **shall we** (راځه چې لاړ شو! 'come on, let's go!'), the quick singular commands friends use with each other, and how Pashto says **I'm on my way**, **I'll be there in ten minutes** and **I was just about to call you**.

grammar.title: Let's and shall we: the 'we' subjunctive
grammar.body:
To suggest doing something together, use the **perfective subjunctive** for 'we' — the same form you met after بايد and چې — ending in **-و** (-u):

لاړ **شو** 'let's go' · و**خورو** 'let's eat' · و**ګورو** 'let's see / let's meet' · و**ګرځو** 'let's walk around'

On its own, with a question mark, it means **'shall we …?'**: چای **وڅښو**؟ 'shall we have some tea?' · چېرته سره **وګورو**؟ 'where shall we meet?'

To turn it into an invitation, put **راځه چې** in front (to one friend), or **راځئ چې** (to several people, or politely): **راځه چې** لاړ شو! 'come on, let's go!'. راځه is the imperfective imperative of راتلل, literally 'come along'.

The **present** for 'we' is a fixed plan, not a suggestion: نن شپه سينما ته **ځو** 'we're going to the cinema tonight'. Compare سينما ته **لاړ شو**؟ 'shall we go to the cinema?'

The trap: don't use به for suggestions — سينما ته **به** لاړ شو is 'we will go to the cinema', a statement.

examples.en: Come on, everyone, let's go for a walk together.
We're going to the park tonight.

grammar.title: Talking to friends: commands in the 'ته' form
grammar.body:
With friends you use **ته**, so commands are singular: **راشه** 'come', **ووايه** 'say', **وګوره** 'look', **لاړ شه** 'go', **کېنه** 'sit'. To a group, to an elder or to a stranger, use the plural / polite form in **-ئ**: راشئ، ووايئ، لاړ شئ، کېنئ. Switching is natural in one breath: احمده، راشه! ماما، تاسو هم راشئ!

**Perfective or imperfective?** The ordinary command is perfective (with و- or a separable part like لاړ / تيار): **راشه** 'come (now)', **زما انتظار وکړه** 'wait for me'. The imperfective form, without و-, is for something ongoing or for *how* to do it: **ورو ځه** 'go slowly', **راځه** 'come along', دلته زما انتظار **کوه** 'keep waiting for me here'.

**Don't.** Negative commands always use **مه** + the **imperfective**: مه **ځه** 'don't go', بيړه مه **کوه** 'don't rush', ناوخته مه **کېږه** 'don't be late'. Never مه وکړه or مه شه.

**Pushing and softening.** Friends add little words: **کنه** 'come on' (راشه کنه! 'oh, come on!'), **نو** 'then' (ووايه نو! 'go on, say it!'), and **ياره**. With elders, wrap the same command in **مهرباني وکړئ** or ask: کولای شئ چې …؟

examples.en: Go on, tell me — what's up?

examples.native: دلته زما انتظار کوه، زه همدا اوس راځم.
examples.roman: dálta zmā intizā́r kawa, zə hamdā́ os rā́dzəm.
examples.en: Wait for me here, I'm coming right now.

grammar.title: On my way, and 'I was just about to …'
grammar.body:
**The present for right now and very soon.** Like English 'I'm coming!', Pashto uses the plain present for what is about to happen: **راځم** 'I'm coming', **رسېږم** 'I'm arriving, I'll be there', لس دقيقې کې **رسېږم** 'I'll be there in ten minutes', فلم اوس شروع **کېږي** 'the film's about to start'. Keep به for things further off or less certain.

**On the way.** **روان يم** 'I'm on my way' (روان 'moving, under way'); **په لار کې يم** 'I'm on the road'; **نږدې يم** 'I'm close'; **تيارېږم** 'I'm getting ready'. When you get there, Pashto uses the past where English says 'I'm here': **ورسېدم** (lit. 'I arrived'), موږ **ورسېدو** 'we're here'.

**'I was just about to …'** Pashto says 'I wanted to …': **ما غوښتل چې** درته زنګ ووهم 'I was just about to call you'. غوښتل is transitive, so the past needs the oblique **ما** (or the clitic: غوښتل **مې** چې …) — not زه. The verb after چې is in the subjunctive.

examples.native: روان يم، پنځه دقيقې کې رسېږم.
examples.roman: rawā́n yəm, pindzə́ daqiqé ke raséẓəm.
examples.en: I'm on my way, I'll be there in five minutes.

examples.native: ما غوښتل چې درته زنګ ووهم!
examples.roman: mā ġuṣtə́l che dərta zang wə́wahəm!
examples.en: I was just about to call you!

examples.native: په لار کې يم، په ټکسي کې ناست يم.
examples.roman: pə lār ke yəm, pə ṭaksí ke nāst yəm.
examples.en: I'm on the road — I'm sitting in a taxi.

culture: Plans between Pashtun friends are loose and generous. Whoever suggests going out usually pays — expect a friendly fight over the bill (more in unit 24). Times are approximate, and 'ten minutes' (لس دقيقې) is a figure of speech; nobody minds much, though teasing the friend who is always late is a sport. A bare **انشاالله** in answer to an invitation can mean 'probably not', so if you really mean yes, say **خامخا** or **حتماً**. In Peshawar people meet at Namak Mandi for karahi and tikka, in Hayatabad's parks or on University Road; in Kabul friends meet in restaurants, in Shahr-e Naw park, or drive out to Qargha and Paghman on Fridays. The weekend is **جمعه** in Afghanistan and Sunday in Pakistan. Friends plan in WhatsApp groups (**ډله**), mixing Pashto with English 'plan', 'OK', 'cancel' — and in Peshawar the Urdu-flavoured **ټيک ده** 'fine' is as common as سمه ده. Groups of friends are usually all men or all women; going out in mixed groups is rare outside big-city universities and offices.

lessons.title: Suggesting what to do

tip.title: Let's … / Shall we …? — the 'we' subjunctive
tip.body:
- **Shall we …?** = the perfective 'we' form + ?: لاړ **شو**؟ وګور**و**؟ وخور**و**؟
- **Let's …!** = **راځه چې** (to one friend) / **راځئ چې** (to a group) + the same form.
- The plain present is a fixed plan: پارک ته **ځو** 'we're going to the park'.
- No به here — به لاړ شو is 'we will go'.
tip.pattern: راځه چې + … لاړ شو / وخورو / وګورو

tip.title: Commands between friends
tip.body:
- With a friend use the **ته** form: راشه، ووايه، لاړ شه. To elders and groups: راشئ، ووايئ، لاړ شئ.
- **Don't** = **مه** + the imperfective: بيړه مه **کوه**، ناوخته مه **کېږه** — never مه وکړه.
- Push with **کنه** (راشه کنه! 'come on!') or **نو** (ووايه نو! 'go on, say it!').

tip.title: I'm on my way: روان يم، رسېږم
tip.body:
- For 'right now / very soon' use the plain present: **راځم** 'I'm coming', لس دقيقې کې **رسېږم** 'I'll be there in ten minutes'.
- **روان يم** 'I'm on my way' · **تيارېږم** 'I'm getting ready' · **ورسېدم** 'I'm here' (lit. I arrived).
- 'I was just about to …' = **ما غوښتل چې** + subjunctive — ما, not زه, because غوښتل is transitive.

sentences.en: We're on our way — you come too.

sentences.native: په سړک کې ډېر موټر دي، ځنډ مې وشو.
sentences.roman: pə saṛák ke ḍer moṭár di, dzanḍ me wə́shu.
sentences.en: There are loads of cars on the road — I got held up.

sentences.native: سمدستي تيار شه، ملګري راغلل!
sentences.roman: samdastí tayā́r sha, malgə́ri rā́ġləl!
sentences.en: Get ready right now — the guys are here!

tip.title: Saying no nicely
tip.body:
- Start with **بښنه غواړم** or **افسوس**.
- Give a reason: بوخت يم، ناروغ يم، مېلمانه لرو 'we've got guests'.
- Offer another time: **بل ځل، انشاالله** or سبا؟
- Careful: a bare **انشاالله** often means 'probably not'. If you mean yes, say **خامخا**.

sentences.native: بښنه غواړم، نن نه شم راتلای، مېلمانه لرو.
sentences.roman: baṣə́na ġwā́ṛəm, nən na shəm rātlā́y, melmā́na láru.
sentences.en: Sorry, I can't come today — we've got guests.

sentences.native: د سبا ملاقات لغوه دی.
sentences.roman: də sabā́ mulāqā́t laġwá day.
sentences.en: Tomorrow's meet-up is off.

sentences.native: پروګرام مو لغوه کړ، ځکه چې باران و.
sentences.roman: prográm mo laġwá kaṛ, dzə́ka che bārā́n wə.
sentences.en: We called it off because it was raining.

sentences.native: دا خو يوه بهانه ده!
sentences.roman: dā xo yáwa bahāná da!
sentences.en: That's just an excuse!

sentences.native: هره ورځ يوه نوې بهانه لرې!
sentences.roman: hára wradz yáwa náwe bahāná lare!
sentences.en: Every day you have a new excuse!

sentences.native: ژمنه دې کړې وه چې راځې!
sentences.roman: zhmána de kṛe wa che rā́dze!
sentences.en: You promised you'd come!

sentences.native: زما ژمنه ده، بله اوونۍ خامخا راځم.
sentences.roman: zmā zhmána da, bə́la owənə́y xāmaxā́ rā́dzəm.
sentences.en: I promise — next week I'll definitely come.

sentences.native: زموږ ډله هره جمعه يو ځای ډوډۍ خوري.
sentences.roman: zmuẓ ḍála hára jumʿá yaw dzāy ḍoḍə́y xwri.
sentences.en: Our gang eats together every Friday.

sentences.native: موږ هره ورځ يو بل ته زنګ وهو.
sentences.roman: muẓ hára wradz yaw bəl ta zang wahú.
sentences.en: We call each other every day.

sentences.native: سمه ده، خير دی، بل ځل.
sentences.roman: sáma da, xayr day, bəl dzal.
sentences.en: OK, never mind — next time.
